plan.angle: Title: 'Plague Case in Russia: What's Confirmed, What's Suspected and How Plague Is Diagnosed (as of Oct 10, 2026)'. Opening beat: as of Oct 8, 2026, the Irkutsk oblast governor said quarantine had been lifted, with nearly 5,000 tests finding no dangerous microorganisms and monitoring of close contacts complete (use his exact figure and wording). WHO says it has asked for more information. Russian authorities describe second-case reports as false (paraphrase, no quote marks). Plague is not confirmed and not ruled out. Then: incubation (CDC: pneumonic 'can be as short as 1 day'; WHO: 1–7 days for Y. pestis), WHO's contact monitoring and 7-day preventive antibiotics given by health authorities, lab diagnosis (culture from blood, sputum or bubo samples, PCR, the WHO-validated rapid dipstick, reference-lab confirmation), and what negative tests in contacts can and can't tell us. Close with the urgent-contact line and 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.'
plan.working_title: Plague Quarantine Lifted in Russia: Why a Week of Watching Contacts Is Enough (as of Oct 10)
plan.why: The quarantine lifted on Oct 8 left a gap between 'over' and 'unexplained' that people are searching to understand, with low competition. It is our first chance at a plague long-form with new depth rather than a repeat of the held decoder. | fact-check: The topic is sound and fits the pillars, but four things need fixing. (1) The title says 'Why a Week of Watching Contacts Is Enough'. That is our own judgement and no agency has said it, while WHO says it still lacks the information it needs. 'Lifted in Russia' is also too wide: the quarantine was in Irkutsk oblast. (2) CDC's signs-and-symptoms page (last reviewed May 15, 2024) says the pneumonic incubation period 'can be as short as 1 day' and gives no upper limit, so CDC can't be the source for 'about a week'. WHO's fact sheet says 'an incubation period of one to seven days' for Y. pestis in general (not specific to pneumonic). WHO also tells authorities to 'identify and monitor close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and give them a seven-day chemoprophylaxis.' Credit each fact to the body that actually says it. (3) I couldn't confirm 'over 90% of contacts' in any source. Liga, UNN and AFP report that Governor Kobzev said nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous microorganisms and that medical monitoring of all close contacts was complete. The Kyiv Independent article I found is the earlier quarantine story. Copy the governor's exact figure from a reachable source and date it to the day he said it (AFP: Thursday, Oct 8). Credit the 'community-acquired pneumonia' diagnosis to the governor, as reported. (4) Some outlets repeat a 'broken test tube' story and say she died 'from pneumonic plague' as if that were fact. Leave both out. On the 'why it ended' question, only report the reasons the governor gave. Don't invent a safety-margin rationale.

package.description:
Plague not confirmed, not ruled out: why the Irkutsk oblast quarantine ended, as of Oct 10, 2026.

Quick answer: On Oct 8, 2026, the Irkutsk oblast governor said nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms and monitoring of all contacts was complete. As of Oct 10 the quarantine is lifted, and Rospotrebnadzor says no plague case has been registered. On Oct 8, WHO said it still didn't know what caused the lab worker's death. Not confirmed is not the same as ruled out.

General information, not medical advice. Possible exposure plus fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. Don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
1. WHO plague fact sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/plague
2. CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Plague: https://www.cdc.gov/plague/hcp/diagnosis-testing/index.html
3. AP via PBS NewsHour: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russias-public-health-watchdog-denies-a-second-infection-in-suspected-pneumonic-plague-case
4. Kyiv Independent: https://kyivindependent.com/russia-lifts-quarantine-in-irkutsk-region-where-lab-worker-allegedly-died-of-plague/

script.working_title: Plague Quarantine Lifted in Irkutsk Oblast: Why, and How Plague Is Diagnosed (as of Oct 10, 2026)
script.hook_pattern: Open loop (dated status decoder). The opening pairs the newest official development (the governor said on Oct 8 that quarantine was lifted) with the official positions: Russian authorities say no plague case has been registered, and on Oct 8 WHO said the cause of death was still unexplained. It then promises to explain what kind of result actually settles a plague question.

scenes.narration: As of Oct 10, 2026, the quarantine in Irkutsk oblast, Russia, has been lifted. Russian authorities say no plague case has been registered. But on Oct 8, WHO said it still didn't know what caused the lab worker's death.

visual.stock_query: calm map Irkutsk oblast with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: the quarantine is over, but the cause is still unexplained

scenes.narration: On Thursday, Oct 8, Irkutsk oblast governor Igor Kobzev said nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had found no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms, and that medical monitoring of all contacts had been completed. That's his statement, as reported by several outlets.
scenes.retention_device: Concrete proof point in the first 15 seconds

scenes.narration: So how does a quarantine end while WHO is still asking what happened? It sounds like a contradiction. It isn't, and the reason comes down to who gets tested, and how plague is tested.
By the end, you'll know what kind of result actually settles a plague question, and why nearly 5,000 negative tests, on their own, can't.

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in 'What negative tests mean'

scenes.retention_device: Trust signal before the deep dive

scenes.narration: Let's sort this into three boxes: what officials have said, what has been reported, and what is still unknown.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a simple framework

scenes.narration: First, the background. In early October, a laboratory worker in Irkutsk oblast died of a severe pneumonia, and reports described it as suspected pneumonic plague.
We won't name her, and we won't speculate about how she got sick. A person died, and that deserves respect.
Russia's federal health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, says she died of pneumonia of unknown origin, AP reported. The regional governor, Igor Kobzev, used the same description, CGTN reported.
scenes.retention_device: New detail many viewers haven't heard

scenes.narration: Then came the second-case reports. Some reports claimed another employee had fallen ill. On Oct 8, Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, denied those reports, AP reported. The same day, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said most media reporting on the situation was false information, Al Jazeera reported.
Also on Oct 8, the World Health Organization said it had asked Russian authorities for more information, including about the reports of a second employee.
scenes.on_screen_text: WHO, OCT 8: ASKED FOR MORE INFO

scenes.narration: Two days earlier, on Oct 6, Russia had told WHO there was no evidence pneumonic plague played a part in her death, and that no pathogens had been detected, UN News reported.
scenes.retention_device: Dated detail that reframes the story

scenes.narration: So here are the boxes as of Oct 10. First, the news from Irkutsk oblast.
Then, the official positions.

items: WHO, Oct 8: asked for more information
Rospotrebnadzor, Oct 8: no plague case registered
WHO, Oct 8: cause of death still unknown

scenes.narration: Notice the gap. Quarantine is over. Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, says no plague case has been registered, and that extensive testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with, AP reported. But on Oct 8, WHO said it still didn't know what caused her death. So plague is not confirmed, and not ruled out. Not confirmed is not the same as ruled out.

visual.myth: Quarantine over = the case is fully explained
visual.fact: Russian authorities: no plague case registered. WHO, Oct 8: cause still unknown

scenes.retention_device: Memorable rule viewers will see again

scenes.narration: The governor gave two reasons for lifting quarantine: the test results, and the monitoring of all contacts, which he said was complete. That's what he said, so that's what we'll stick to.

items: Governor: nearly 5,000 tests, no dangerous microorganisms
Governor: monitoring of all contacts complete

scenes.retention_device: Sets up the two science sections

scenes.narration: What we can do is explain the science behind both of those reasons. And it starts with a clock.
Every infection has a gap between exposure and the first symptoms. That gap is called the incubation period.
Plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis. It comes in three forms: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic, the form that affects the lungs.

visual.stock_query: rod shaped bacteria cartoon under microscope

scenes.narration: For plague in general, WHO says infected people usually develop symptoms after an incubation period of 1 to 7 days.
For pneumonic plague specifically, CDC says the incubation period can be as short as 1 day.

visual.stat_label: Pneumonic incubation can be this short (CDC)

scenes.narration: That speed matters, because pneumonic plague is the form that can spread from person to person, through respiratory droplets during close contact.

visual.stock_query: two people talking close with droplet dots

scenes.narration: Bubonic plague, by contrast, is usually spread by the bite of an infected flea.
So the people at risk from a pneumonic case are the ones who were close to the patient, which is why health authorities focus on close contacts.

visual.myth: Pneumonic plague spreads through the air like measles
visual.fact: It spreads through respiratory droplets during close contact (CDC, WHO)
visual.stock_query: small circle of people highlighted on map

scenes.retention_device: Myth correction of a circulating belief

scenes.narration: Now, the flip side of that fast clock. WHO says pneumonic plague can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours if it isn't treated. But recovery rates are high when it's detected and treated in time, within 24 hours of symptoms starting.

visual.stat_label: Treated within this window: high recovery (WHO)

scenes.narration: And CDC says plague is treatable with commonly available antibiotics. The earlier treatment starts, the better the chances of a full recovery.
So who exactly gets watched, and what does watching involve? This is where WHO's guidance gets very specific.
Here's WHO's instruction to health authorities, word for word: identify and monitor close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and give them a seven-day chemoprophylaxis.

visual.quote: Identify and monitor close contacts of pneumonic plague patients and give them a seven-day chemoprophylaxis.
visual.attribution: World Health Organization, Plague fact sheet
visual.stock_query: public health office with map board

scenes.retention_device: Real quote from the primary source

scenes.narration: Chemoprophylaxis just means preventive antibiotics. In plain terms: find the people who were close to the patient, watch their health, and give them a 7-day course.
That's a 7-day course, set by WHO for close contacts of pneumonic plague patients.

visual.stat_label: Preventive antibiotic course for close contacts (WHO)

scenes.narration: Watching means checking for early warning signs, so anyone who becomes ill can be isolated and treated fast.
CDC lists the signs of pneumonic plague: fever, headache and weakness, then a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and cough, sometimes with bloody or watery mucus.
One important point: this is done by health authorities, with prescribed medicines. It's not a do-it-yourself plan, so please don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics.
This playbook has been tested in a big way. In 2017, Madagascar had an unusual urban outbreak, mostly pneumonic plague, in cities including the capital, Antananarivo.

visual.stock_query: map of Madagascar with city pin

scenes.narration: Between August and November 2017, 2,414 clinically suspected plague cases were reported, and 1,878 of them were classified as pneumonic.

visual.stat_label: Clinically suspected plague cases, Madagascar, Aug–Nov 2017

scenes.narration: Contact tracing and preventive antibiotics for contacts were part of the response.

visual.stock_query: health workers with clipboards visiting homes

scenes.narration: But here's where it gets weird. Of the 1,878 pneumonic cases, only 32, about 2%, were confirmed by a laboratory. 386 were probable.

visual.stock_query: small pile versus big pile of folders

scenes.narration: The rest were suspected cases based on symptoms. Which raises the real question of this video: how do you actually prove it's plague?

visual.stock_query: three level ladder suspected probable confirmed

scenes.narration: For most of history, you couldn't. Plague was judged by symptoms alone, until 1894, when Alexandre Yersin identified the bacterium in Hong Kong.
Today, WHO says confirming plague requires laboratory testing. Fever and cough have many possible causes, so symptoms alone can't settle it.
WHO's best practice is to identify Yersinia pestis in a sample: pus from a swollen lymph node, called a bubo, blood, or sputum, the mucus coughed up from the lungs.
Labs have three main tools, plus a final step.
Tool one: culture. The lab tries to grow the bacteria from the sample and identify them. It's a classic way to confirm plague, but growing bacteria takes time, so it isn't an instant answer.
There's a catch. CDC advises clinicians to collect samples before starting antibiotics where possible, but not to delay treatment for a suspected case.
Tool two: PCR. Instead of growing the bacteria, PCR looks for their genetic material. It's the same basic idea as the COVID PCR tests many of us got to know.
Tool three comes with a great story. Researchers working in Madagascar developed a dipstick that detects a plague protein called F1 antigen, with results in up to 15 minutes.
Their study, published in The Lancet in 2003, tested a quick dipstick designed to be used in the field, not just in big city labs.

visual.stock_query: small rural clinic with test kit

scenes.narration: Today, WHO describes a laboratory-validated rapid dipstick test now widely used in Africa and South America.

visual.stock_query: globe highlighting Africa and South America

scenes.narration: A rapid test is fast, but it's a screening step. Positive results still need lab confirmation, which is why Madagascar counted rapid-test positives as probable, not confirmed.

visual.myth: A positive rapid test confirms plague
visual.fact: In Madagascar 2017, it counted as probable until lab methods confirmed it
visual.stock_query: test strip next to lab microscope

scenes.narration: And the final step: in the US, CDC tells clinicians who suspect plague to notify local and state health departments immediately, take samples before treatment if possible, and never delay treatment while waiting for results.
There's also antibody testing, which looks for the body's immune response. But antibodies take time to build up, so it isn't the fast answer.
Put simply: lab confirmation means finding the bacterium, its genetic material or its proteins, in samples from the patient. Hold that thought.
scenes.retention_device: 'Hold that thought' sets up the payoff

scenes.narration: Because now we can answer the big question. What do nearly 5,000 negative tests actually tell us?

visual.stock_query: mountain of test tubes with question mark

scenes.retention_device: Returns to the main open loop

scenes.narration: Start with what the governor said: nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous microorganisms.

The reports we found don't break down who or what was sampled, or which methods were used. And some reporting on this case can't be checked: the Kyiv Independent, for example, says it could not independently verify reports about staff being confined at the institute. So we'll keep our reading to what officials said.
What negative results can tell you: in the samples tested, the dangerous microorganisms they were looking for weren't found.

visual.stock_query: green check marks on sample rack

scenes.narration: Together with the monitoring of contacts, which the governor said was complete, that's the basis he gave for lifting quarantine. It's reassuring information about the samples that were tested.

What they can't tell you on their own: what made her sick. Tests on contacts are tests on other people. Rospotrebnadzor says extensive testing found no evidence her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with, AP reported. But in the reports we found, the methods and results haven't been published, and WHO says it is still seeking information.

visual.stock_query: two separate folders labeled patient contacts

scenes.narration: Think of a smoke alarm in the house next door. A silent alarm there is good news about next door. For the first house, you need its own alarm log, and it has to be shared.

visual.stock_query: two cartoon houses with smoke alarms

scenes.narration: And any test only reflects the sample it was given, and when that sample was taken. CDC advises clinicians to collect samples before starting antibiotics where possible, without ever delaying treatment.

So here's the payoff. What settles a plague question is lab evidence from the patient's own samples, using methods like culture, PCR or antigen tests, shared openly enough for bodies like WHO to assess. Russian authorities say no plague case has been registered. WHO says it is still seeking information.

visual.stock_query: key unlocking box with test tube

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: As of Oct 10, 2026: Russian authorities say no plague case has been registered. WHO has not confirmed plague and says it is still seeking information. The cause of her death has not been publicly explained.
scenes.on_screen_text: OCT 10: NOT CONFIRMED, NOT RULED OUT

visual.stat_label: Russian authorities: no plague case; WHO seeking info

scenes.narration: Myth one: quarantine lifted means the question is closed. Not quite. The governor cited negative tests and completed contact monitoring. Russian authorities say no plague case was registered, but WHO is still seeking information.

visual.myth: Quarantine lifted means the case is fully explained
visual.fact: The governor cited negative tests and completed contact monitoring; WHO is still seeking information

scenes.narration: Myth two: plague has no cure. CDC says plague is treatable with commonly available antibiotics, and WHO says recovery rates are high when it's treated in time.

visual.fact: Treatable with commonly available antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC)

scenes.narration: And a calming fact from the US: CDC says person-to-person spread of plague has not been documented there since 1924.

visual.stat_label: No documented US person-to-person spread since (CDC)

scenes.narration: Here's your checklist for reading every plague headline.
One: not confirmed is not ruled out. Two: check the date on every status line, because it changes fast.

Three: credit the body that actually said it, the governor, Rospotrebnadzor, WHO or CDC. Four: negative tests in contacts are not a diagnosis of the patient, so look for the patient's own results, shared openly.
And the one that matters most: if you've had a possible exposure, such as close contact with someone suspected of pneumonic plague, or time in an area where plague occurs, watch for warning signs.
scenes.retention_device: Escalation to the most important point

scenes.narration: Fever, cough, shortness of breath or chest pain, or a sudden painful swollen lymph node? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently, and tell them about the exposure.
Don't self-treat or stockpile antibiotics. Treatment for plague comes from a clinician, and CDC says the earlier it starts, the better the chances of a full recovery.

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient talking in clinic

scenes.narration: So, as of Oct 10, 2026: quarantine in Irkutsk oblast is lifted. The governor said nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous microorganisms and that monitoring of all contacts was complete. Rospotrebnadzor says no plague case has been registered. And on Oct 8, WHO said it still didn't know what caused her death, and it is seeking more information.

factcheck.summary:
The structure, tone, safety lines and most of the science hold up. Fourteen sources resolve and support their lines, and two more (S7 and S8) are confirmed through search results only (details below). Checked claims include WHO's 1–7 days, 18–24 h, the 24 h window and the seven-day chemoprophylaxis quote; CDC's "as short as 1 day", the pneumonic signs, "1924", "commonly available antibiotics" and "notify, sample, don't delay"; the Madagascar figures (2,414 / 1,878 / 32 / 386); the Chanteau 2003 15-minute F1 dipstick; Yersin in Hong Kong in 1894; Russia's Oct 6 message to WHO (UN News); Rospotrebnadzor's Thursday Oct 8 denial (AP); Peskov (Al Jazeera, Oct 8); and the governor's figures (CGTN).

There are three fixable problems:
1. **Wrong date for a WHO statement.** AP says Van Kerkhove said WHO "doesn't know what caused" the death on Wednesday, which is Oct 7, 2026. The script dates it Oct 8 in five places.
2. **Diagnosis overstated, and the script contradicts itself.** s53 and s62 present antigen and DNA detection as confirmation. But s50 correctly says a rapid antigen positive is only "probable", and CDC's 2020 case definition lists PCR and antigen detection as presumptive. Confirmatory evidence is culture isolation or a fourfold antibody change.
3. **Source tags don't say their lines.** S5 never mentions PCR, antigen tests or culture taking time. S12 (UNN) credits the "nearly 5,000 tests" to Rospotrebnadzor specialists, not the governor.

No newer official status turned up for Oct 9–10. Recheck at publish time.

issues.location: s01, s14 (list item 3), s15, s73 (narration + list item 5), hook_pattern
issues.claim: On Oct 8, WHO said it still didn't know what caused the lab worker's death.
issues.problem: The source cited (S13, AP, published Oct 8, 2026) says: "On Wednesday, Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the U.N. health agency doesn't know what caused the woman's Oct. 2 death." Wednesday is Oct 7, 2026. That's the same mistake that got L1 10-09 held: crediting a statement to the wrong day. Only WHO's request for more information, including about the second-employee reports, is dated Oct 8 (Al Jazeera, S15).
issues.fix: Change every instance to Oct 7. s01: "But on Oct 7, WHO said it still didn't know what caused the lab worker's death." s14 list item 3: "WHO, Oct 7: cause of death still unknown". s15: "But on Oct 7, WHO said it still didn't know what caused her death." s73: "And on Oct 7, WHO said it still didn't know what caused her death, and on Oct 8 it said it had asked for more information." s73 list item 5: "WHO, Oct 7: cause still unknown; Oct 8: asked for more info". hook_pattern: "on Oct 7 WHO said the cause of death was still unexplained". Set source_ids for these lines to S13.

issues.claim: Lab confirmation means finding the bacterium, its genetic material or its proteins in samples from the patient. What settles it is lab evidence using methods like culture, PCR or antigen tests.
issues.problem: This contradicts s50, which says a rapid antigen positive is "probable", not confirmed. Under CDC's 2020 plague case definition, detecting Y. pestis DNA or antigens (PCR, DFA, F1 antigen) is presumptive evidence. Confirmatory evidence is culture isolation validated by a second assay, or a fourfold change between paired antibody samples. The script also leaves out paired serology as a way to confirm. As written, it overstates what a single PCR or antigen result proves.
issues.fix: s53 narration: "Put simply: fast tests like PCR and antigen tests look for the bacterium's genetic material or proteins and give strong clues. Under CDC's case definition, confirmation means growing the bacterium from the patient's own sample, or seeing antibodies rise between two blood samples taken weeks apart. Hold that thought." s53 on-screen: "PROOF COMES FROM THE PATIENT" (unchanged). s62 narration: "So here's the payoff. What settles a plague question is lab results from the patient's own samples, such as culture or antibody tests backed by fast tests like PCR, shared openly enough for bodies like WHO to assess. Russian authorities say no plague case has been registered. WHO says it is still seeking information." Add source S17 (CDC case definition, below) to s53 and s62.

issues.location: s42, s43, s45, s53, s62 (source_ids S5)
issues.claim: CDC (S5) supports: culture takes time; PCR looks for genetic material; antigen tests.
issues.problem: The CDC Clinical Testing and Diagnosis page (S5, reviewed Oct 7, 2026) covers notification, pre-treatment specimens, blood cultures, stains and paired serology. It does not mention PCR, F1 antigen or rapid tests, and it doesn't say culture takes time. These source tags don't say their lines.
issues.fix: Add S17: "Plague (Yersinia pestis) 2020 Case Definition", CDC National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System, 2020, https://ndc.services.cdc.gov/case-definitions/plague-2020. It mentions PCR and antigen detection. Add S18: "Rapid diagnostic tests for plague (protocol)", Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Jullien S, et al.), 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6804290. It says "Results from culture and paired serology take several days". s43 source_ids: ["S5","S18"]. s45 source_ids: ["S17"]. s42 source_ids: ["S2","S5","S8","S17"]. s52 source_ids: ["S5","S18"].

hold_reason: Dropped by Editor-in-Chief: Three major fact-check problems are unresolved. thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates are clean, single-focal-point designs with legible text at phone size. The title poses a direct question ("Why?") about the quarantine ending. #0 ("THE 7-DAY CLOCK / WHY IT ENDED") most tightly mirrors that question — it teases a concrete mechanism (the incubation/monitoring window) without giving away the answer, creating the strongest curiosity gap while staying calm and non-sensational. #1 ("5,000") is a strong, credible number but is about testing volume, a related but secondary fact that doesn't directly answer why the quarantine ended. #2 ("HOW THEY TEST") shifts the topic to diagnostic methods, which is a plausible video angle but reads as a mismatch against the "why ended" title, likely weakening click intent even though it's well executed. #0 best balances relevance, curiosity, and legibility.
